en: Preface to the Ninth Assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the "Vajracchedikā" Section, composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery.
I have humbly investigated that those whose source is vast and overflowing must necessarily store up the most wondrous and numinous; those whose peaks are intricate and tangled...
This is the spontaneous unfolding of the contemplation of the profound and mysterious.

How much more so when the illuminating radiance is clearly manifest and the transcendent resonance rises far aloft; when the pattern of the True is embodied and the knot of the Mysterious establishes the ultimate; when the Great Divination (Dànyàn) takes root in the primal assembly and the Minor Accomplishment (Xiǎochéng) is transformed in the subsequent mind; and when spiritual power is stored and blessings are accumulated—truly, this is most fitting!
Therefore, in his seizing of opportune moments and articulation of essential points, his three questions to Jie reached their pinnacle;
in his discernment of principles and the pathways of emotion, his two "As" (Aḥ) attained their ultimate refinement.
He exhausted the realm of non-conceptualization to manifest conceptual thought, thereby magnifying the great achievement of that which cannot be saved.
Gathering the multitude through the perfection of giving, he encourages the vast virtue of those who have not yet practiced.
May his vows be like the bright sun, reaching the void of space beyond measure;
may his faith be like the wind, wafting fragrance and sound without lingering.
If one forgets the Dharma-body within its marks and signs, how can one see the Tathāgata?
If one divides the Buddha-lands into minute dust motes, what constitutes a world?

The number of sands in the Ganges is not the "many" of true merit; the mountain king is not the "great" of a great body. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) transcends words; to claim it exists is to slander it.
Awakening is free from grasping; it is realized by knowing that there is nothing to bestow.

It is for this reason that one brushes away the mists at the ford of doubt and cuts off the sprouts on the path of the mind. One appreciates the resonance with all things without limit, and while cherishing the flow of circumstances and emotions, one must bring them to their ultimate end.
Yet the sharpness of the vajra can consume two objects;
its fierce power of counter-elimination leaves not even a single thought unobstructed.
Since these words must address generalities, my expressions are for the most part concise.
The principles are profound and subtle, which is why the minds of many are prone to confusion.

It was for this reason that the sages of antiquity composed their treatises and the worthies of later generations devoted themselves to intensive study; it was not merely because there was a karmic affinity with China, but truly because these teachings were held in high esteem during this auspicious era.
There are two versions, one extensive and one abbreviated, comprising five translations in total; they are neither new nor old, becoming increasingly refined and clear with each successive version.

Since the presence of these sutra scrolls is equivalent to the presence of the Buddha, the traces of those who receive and uphold them yield miraculous efficacy. The transmission of this fact to all who hear it is fully detailed in the separate record.
It sweeps away the two extremes and clarifies the nine contemplations: cloud-like hair flows with whiskers, harboring the shadows of sorrowful transformation and extinction;
lightning-swift eyes like pearls reflect the fleeting light of flourishing and transition.
When the stars gather at night and fall as dawn breaks, false views are difficult to maintain;
when dew glistens in the shade and dries in the sun, the accumulation of peril is but brief.

Since conditioned phenomena are thus, and unconditioned reality is likewise, how could one fail to receive the profound grace of the entrustment and personally attain the sublime realization of its practice?
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 577.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
The Ninth Chapter, "The Vajra that Severes": Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One adjusted his robes, took up his bowl and outer garment, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having finished his alms-round through the city, the Blessed One returned to his original location. After eating and putting away his bowl and robe, he washed his feet; then, in the afternoon, he spread out his seat as usual, sat down cross-legged, straightened his body, set his intention correctly, and dwelt in mindfulness directed toward the present.

At that time, the bhikṣus came to where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side. The Venerable Subhūti was also seated within this assembly.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous!
Blessed One!

Even unto the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is able to embrace all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with the most supreme embracing; even unto the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is able to entrust all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with the most supreme entrusting.
"Bhagavān! Those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle—how should they dwell?
How should they practice?"
"How does one subdue and control the mind?
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One then addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent, Subhūti! It is so! It is thus!
So it is! It is as you have said.

Even the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to embrace all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with the most supreme embrace; even the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to entrust all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with the most supreme entrustment.

Therefore, Subhūti, you should listen attentively and apply your mind with great care; I shall analyze and explain for you how those who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle should abide, how they should practice, and how they should subdue their minds.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! All those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle should give rise to this thought:
‘All sentient beings—those comprised within the category of sentient beings;’”

Whether born from an egg, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception; even unto the conceptualization and that which is conceptually designated within the realm of sentient beings.

I shall cause all such beings as these to attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of wondrous nirvana without remainder; yet, although I have thus delivered immeasurable sentient beings to extinction, there is not a single sentient being who has attained extinction.
Why is that? Subhūti!
If the notion of a "sentient being" arises in bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they should not be called bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Why is that? Subhūti!
If bodhisattva mahāsattvas are present, one should not say that the perception of sentient beings arises.

In the same way, one should know that the notions of a life-principle (*jīva*), a person (*pudgala*), an individual (*puruṣa*), a spirit-born (*manuja*), a descendant of Manu (*mānava*), an agent (*kartṛ*), and an experiencer (*vedaka*) likewise arise.
Why is that? Subhūti!
There is not even the slightest dharma that can be called one who has set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice giving without dwelling on things; he should practice giving without dwelling anywhere at all.
He should practice giving without dwelling on form; he should practice giving without dwelling on sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena."
"Subhūti! In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice giving without dwelling upon the perception of signs. Why is that?"
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without dwelling anywhere at all, that mass of merit cannot be measured.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think? Can the space in the eastern direction be measured? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! " "Excellent, Subhūti!"
"In this way, throughout the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below— pervading all worlds in the ten directions—
is the space of those worlds measurable? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Sudhana!”
"So it is! So it is! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without dwelling on anything at all, the mass of his merit is likewise immeasurable."
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva should thus practice giving without dwelling upon the perception of signs.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the possession of the various marks? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
One should not view the Tathāgata by means of the possession of various marks."
Why is this? Because what the Tathāgata calls the possession of all marks is itself not the possession of all marks.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha again addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Subhūti! All that is endowed with marks is false; all that is not endowed with marks is not false. In this way, one should view the Tathāgata by means of both marks and the absence of marks."
When these words had been spoken, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,

saying: “World-Honored One, will there be sentient beings in a future age, in a later time, in the final five hundred years, when the period of the extinction of the True Dharma is unfolding, who, upon hearing such scriptural passages as these concerning form, will give rise to the perception of reality?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Do not speak thus:

'Will there be any sentient beings in a future age, at a later time, in the final five hundred years, when the period of the extinction of the True Dharma is unfolding, who, upon hearing such words and phrases of this sūtra as these, will conceive of them as true?'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the future age, in the later time, in the final period, during the five hundred years when the True Dharma is about to perish; they will be fully endowed with ethical discipline, endowed with virtue, and endowed with wisdom."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not served and made offerings to only one Buddha, nor have they planted roots of goodness under only one Buddha."
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must have served and made offerings to more than just one, a hundred, or a thousand Buddhas, and planted roots of goodness under more than just one, a hundred, or a thousand Buddhas, before they can hear such words and phrases from a sūtra as these and attain a single pure faith.
"Subhūti! The Tathāgata has fully known them all with his Buddha-wisdom; the Tathāgata has fully seen them all with his Buddha-eye. Subhūti!"
The Tathāgata has fully awakened to all this.
All sentient beings shall produce immeasurable and incalculable masses of merit, and they shall gather immeasurable and incalculable masses of merit. Why is this?

"Subhūti! That bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to the notion of a self; he does not give rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-force, the notion of a person, the notion of a soul, the notion of a mind-born being, the notion of a manava, the notion of an agent, or the notion of an experiencer."

"Subhūti! That bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to the perception of dharmas, nor does he give rise to the perception of non-dharmas; he does not give rise to perception, nor does he give rise to non-perception. Why is this so?

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the notion of a phenomenon (dharma-saṃjñā), he would thereby have attachment to a self, attachment to a sentient being, attachment to a life-principle, and attachment to a person, and so forth."

If there were the occurrence of an improper conception, that too would entail the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being, the grasping at a life-principle, and the grasping at a person (pudgala), and so forth. Why is this?
"Subhūti! One should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas; for this reason, the Tathāgata has spoken with intentional meaning regarding the dharma-gate of the raft parable.
Those who possess wisdom should even abandon dharmas, let alone non-dharmas!"
The Buddha again addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
Is there even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized as anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi?
Is there even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught?
Subhūti replied, “World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized as anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; nor is there even the slightest dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
The dharmas realized, taught, and contemplated by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha are all ungraspable and inexpressible; they are neither dharma nor non-dharma.
"Why is this? Because all noble individuals (*pudgala*) are manifested by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"What do you think? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take this trichiliocosm, filled to the brim with the seven precious jewels, and offer it as a gift, would the mass of merit arising from that cause for this son or daughter of good family be great?"
Subhūti replied, “Very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so,
Sugata! By this causal condition, the mass of merit produced by that son or daughter of good family would be exceedingly great."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
As for "a mass of merit, a mass of merit," the Tathāgata has said that it is not a mass of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "a mass of merit, a mass of merit."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying:
“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take this trichiliocosm, filled to the brim with the seven kinds of precious jewels, and offer it as a gift.”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate even a single four-line verse of this Dharma-gate, and furthermore were to extensively proclaim, reveal, and correctly attend to it for others—for this reason, the mass of merit produced would be far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.

Why is this? Because the unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas emerges from this sūtra; all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are born from this sūtra.
Why is that? Subhūti!
What are called the dharmas of the Buddhas are, according to the Tathāgata, not dharmas of the Buddhas; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them as "the dharmas of the Buddhas."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry ever form such a thought as this:"
"Can I realize the fruit of stream-entry? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"Blessed One!
Those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry do not entertain the thought:
'I am able to realize the fruit of stream-entry.'"
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
Those who have entered the stream have not entered into anything at all; therefore, they are called "stream-enterers."
Because they do not enter into form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena, they are called "stream-enterers.
World-Honored One!
If a stream-enterer were to have such a thought:
"If I were to think, 'I have realized the fruit of stream-entry,' that would be for me to grasp at a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a person,
or an individual. The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think?"
"Do those who are once-returners ever think:
'Am I able to realize the fruit of a once-returner? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Those who are once-returners do not form such a thought:”
"I am able to realize the fruit of once-returning. Why is this?
World-Honored One!"
"Because there is not even the slightest dharma by which one realizes the state of a Once-returner, he is therefore called a 'Once-returner'.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
"Do those who are non-returners ever think:
'Am I able to realize the fruit of non-returning? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Those who are Non-returners do not form such a thought:..."
"I am able to realize the fruit of non-returning. Why is this?
World-Honored One!"
"Because there is not even the slightest dharma by which one realizes the nature of a non-returner, he is therefore called a 'non-returner'.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
"Do the Arhats ever have this thought:
'I am able to realize arhatship'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Arhats do not form such a thought: [that they have attained parinirvāṇa]."
"I am able to realize the state of an Arhat. Why is this?
World-Honored One!"
Because there is not even the slightest dharma that can be called "Arhat," for this reason he is named "Arhat.
World-Honored One,
if an Arhat were to form such a thought:
If I were to realize the state of arhatship, that would constitute grasping at a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a person, or a pudgala. Why is this so?
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has declared that I am foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention (*araṇāvihārin*). World-Honored One!
Although I am an arhat forever free from lustful desire, I have never entertained such a thought as this:”
"I have attained arhatship and am forever free from lustful desire.
World-Honored One!
If I were to entertain such a thought as this:"
If I have attained arhatship and am forever free from craving, the Tathāgata should not have predicted of me, saying:
"The noble son Subhūti is foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention."
Because there is absolutely no abiding, the Tathāgata speaks of it as ‘the dwelling in non-contention, the dwelling in non-contention.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: ‘What do you think?’
“When the Tathāgata was formerly in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara,
did he grasp even the slightest dharma? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata was formerly in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, there was not even the slightest dharma that he took up.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there is a bodhisattva who speaks thus:
'I shall accomplish the adornment of the merits of a buddha-field,' such a bodhisattva does not speak the truth."
Why is this? Subhūti!

What is called the "adornment of the qualities of a buddha-field" is, according to the Tathāgata, not an adornment; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "adornment of the qualities of a buddha-field."

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should thus generate a mind that abides nowhere at all. He should generate a mind that does not abide in form, nor should he generate a mind that abides in what is not form; he should generate a mind that does not abide in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor should he generate a mind that abides in what is not sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; he should generate a mind that abides nowhere at all.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Suppose there were a man with a great body; his physical form, by way of illustration, were like Sumeru, the king of mountains. Subhūti!”
"What do you think? Is that self-nature vast? Subhūti replied:
“His very self is vast! World-Honored One, it is vast!”
Well-gone One!
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
"The self-nature of that, the Tathāgata says, is not a self-nature; it is called 'self-nature' precisely because it is not that [inherently existent] nature.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"

Even as many as the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā—suppose there were as many Gaṅgā rivers as there are grains of sand in those [very] Gaṅgā rivers; would the grains of sand in all those Gaṅgā rivers be numerous?"
Subhūti replied, “Very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Very many, Sugata!
The Ganges rivers themselves are already countless, how much more so their sands!"
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!

I now tell you and awaken you to this: suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven kinds of exquisite jewels and offer them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Would the mass of merit produced by this son or daughter of good family on account of this cause and condition be great?"
Subhūti replied, “Very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so,
Sugata! By this cause and condition, the mass of merit produced by that son or daughter of good family would be exceedingly great."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:
"If one were to fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand with the seven precious treasures and offer them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate even a single four-line verse of this Dharma-gate, and furthermore were to extensively proclaim, reveal, and correctly attend to it for others—for this cause and condition, the mass of merit produced would be far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there is any place where this Dharma-gate is even taught or explained to others as a single four-line verse, that place shall be honored by the gods, humans, and asuras of the world as if it were a shrine to the Buddha. How much more so for those who are able to fully master this Dharma-gate—writing it down, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, mastering it thoroughly, and extensively teaching, explaining, and correctly reflecting upon it for others!"
In this way, sentient beings accomplish the most supreme and rare merit.
This place is where the Great Teacher dwelt, or each individual venerable location, or wherever there are those who possess wisdom and fellow practitioners of the holy life.
When he had spoken these words, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this Dharma discourse be named?”
"How should I uphold it?
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable One!"
Now this Dharma gate is named "The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā that Can Sever"; you should uphold it by this name. Why is this?
Subhūti! This perfection of wisdom is what the Tathāgata calls "non-perfection of wisdom"; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "perfection of wisdom."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is there even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has taught?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata can speak.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Would the dust motes of the great earth within a trichiliocosm be many?"
Subhūti replied, “The atoms of dust in this earth, World-Honored One, are exceedingly many!”
"Very many, Sugata! the Buddha said.
“Subhūti! The dust motes of the great earth, the Tathāgata says, are not dust motes; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them by the designation ‘dust motes of the great earth.
All worlds, the Tathāgata says, are not worlds; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them by the designation ‘worlds.’”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Should one view the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
"The thirty-two marks of a great man, which the Tathāgata has described as being non-marks, are therefore called by the Tathāgata 'the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying:

"Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, on each successive day, gave away as many of their own bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and continued giving away their own bodies in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River."

Furthermore, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, regarding this Dharma-gate, even as little as a single four-line stanza, receive, uphold, read, recite, master it thoroughly, and extensively proclaim, reveal, and correctly attend to it for others—for this cause and condition, the mass of merit produced will be far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, moved by the power of the Dharma he had heard, wept and shed tears; bowing his head and wiping away his tears, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous and extraordinary!
World-Honored One!
Most exceedingly rare! Sugata!

The Dharma gate now taught by the Tathāgata universally brings about all manner of benefit for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle; it universally brings about all manner of benefit for those who have set out upon the Most Excellent Vehicle.
"Bhagavān! Since the time I first gave birth to wisdom, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate. Bhagavān!"
If sentient beings, upon hearing such a profound sutra as this, give rise to the thought that it is true, you should know that they have accomplished something most excellent and rare. Why is this?

"Bhagavān! That which is called the 'conception of reality' by those who conceive of reality, the Tathāgata has declared to be non-conception; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the 'conception of reality,' the 'conception of reality.'"
"Bhagavān! It is not particularly rare for me now, having heard this Dharma-gate, to have attained realization, faith, and understanding.

However, if sentient beings in a future age, during the final period, the latter part, the last five hundred years, when the True Dharma is about to perish, should attain realization, faith, and understanding regarding such a profound Dharma-gate; should uphold, read, recite, and master it thoroughly; and should extensively proclaim, reveal, and correctly attend to it for others—it should be known that they achieve what is most supremely rare."
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Those sentient beings do not give rise to the notion of a self; they do not give rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-principle, the notion of a person, the notion of a pudgala, the notion of a mind-born being, the notion of a manava, the notion of an agent, or the notion of a recipient.
Why is this so? World-Honored One!

All notions of a self are actually non-notions; all notions of a sentient being, a life-principle, a spirit, a person, an individual, a mind-born being, a youth, an agent, and an experiencer are actually non-notions.
"Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are free from all conceptualizations.
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One then addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"So it is! So it is, Subhūti!"
If any sentient beings, upon hearing such a profound sutra as this, are not startled, not terrified, and free from fear, you should know that they have accomplished what is most supremely rare.
Why is this? Subhūti!
That which the Tathāgata calls the supreme pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā.
"Subhūti! That which the Tathāgata calls the supreme pāramitā is that which has been proclaimed by immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; therefore, it is named the supreme pāramitā."
The Tathāgata has said that the supreme pāramitā is not a pāramitā; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "supreme pāramitā.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Tathāgata says that the perfection of patience is not a perfection; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "perfection of patience. Why is this?

"Subhūti! In the past, in a former life, when King Kali severed my limbs and flesh, at that time I had no perception of a self, nor a perception of a sentient being, nor a perception of a life-principle, nor a perception of a person, nor a perception of a soul, nor a perception of a mind-born being, nor a perception of a youth, nor a perception of an agent, nor a perception of an experiencer. At that time, I had no perception whatsoever, yet it was not that I lacked perception."
Why is this? Subhūti!
If at that time I had the notion of a self, then at that time I would have had the notion of aversion;

If, at that time, I had any notion of a sentient being, a life-principle, a person, an individual, a mind-born being, a descendant of Manu, an agent, or an experiencer, then at that time I would have had a notion of malice.
Why is this? Subhūti!

I recall that during five hundred past lives, I once styled myself the "Seer of Endurance. At that time, I had no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-principle, no notion of a person, no notion of a pudgala, no notion of a mind-born being, no notion of a manava, no notion of an agent, and no notion of an experiencer. At that time, I had no notions at all, yet it was not that I had no notions.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having distanced themselves from all perceptions, should resolve their mind upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). They should generate that mind without dwelling on form; they should generate that mind without dwelling on what is not form. They should generate that mind without dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharma*); they should generate that mind without dwelling on what is not sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. They should generate that mind without dwelling anywhere at all.
Why is this? Subhūti! Whatever there is that has a dwelling is, in fact, non-dwelling.

For this reason, the Tathāgata says that all bodhisattvas should practice giving without dwelling on anything; they should not practice giving while dwelling on forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
For the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice giving by means of such renunciation."
Why is this? Subhūti!
The notion of a "sentient being" is itself no-notion; it is non-existent.
"All sentient beings," the Tathāgata says, "are non-sentient beings. Subhūti!
The Tathāgata is one who speaks truth, one who speaks reality, one who speaks as it is, and one whose speech does not differ from the fact.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Regarding the dharmas realized by the Tathāgata through direct presence, or the dharmas he has taught, or the dharmas he has contemplated—within these, there is neither truth nor falsehood."

"Subhūti! For example, it is as if a man enters a dark room and sees nothing at all; you should know that it is likewise with a bodhisattva who falls into [the notion of] things—that is, who practices giving while falling into [the notion of] things."

"Subhūti! It is just as when a man with clear vision, having passed through the night until dawn, sees various forms when the sun rises; you should know that it is likewise for a bodhisattva not to fall into [the perception of] things—that is, to practice giving without falling into the perception of things."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate this Dharma-gate, and furthermore extensively proclaim, reveal, and attend to it correctly for others, then the Tathāgata knows such a person with his Buddha-wisdom; the Tathāgata sees such a person with his Buddha-eye; and the Tathāgata fully awakens to such a person."
In this way, all these sentient beings shall generate an immeasurable mass of merit.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to give away as many of their own bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River during the first part of the day; and again give away as many of their own bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River during the middle part of the day; and likewise give away as many of their own bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River during the latter part of the day—thus giving away their own bodies through this method for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

If there are those who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, do not give rise to slander, the mass of merit produced by this cause and condition is already far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable; how much more so for those who can, regarding such a Dharma-gate, fully perfect it, write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, master it thoroughly, and extensively proclaim, reveal, and correctly attend to it for others!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
This Dharma-gate is inconceivable and immeasurable; one should aspire for the inconceivable maturation it brings forth."

"Subhūti! The Tathāgata proclaims such a Dharma gate for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle, and for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings who have set out upon the Most Excellent Vehicle."

"Subhūti! If there are those who take up, uphold, read, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate this Dharma-gate, and furthermore extensively proclaim, reveal, and correctly attend to it for others, then the Tathāgata knows these persons with his Buddha-wisdom; the Tathāgata sees these persons with his Buddha-eye; and the Tathāgata fully awakens to these persons."
In this way, all these sentient beings will achieve an immeasurable mass of merit; they shall all achieve an inconceivable, unfathomable, and boundless mass of merit.
"Subhūti! All these sentient beings bear upon their shoulders the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?"

Subhūti! This Dharma gate cannot be heard by sentient beings of inferior faith and understanding; it cannot be heard by those with the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a person, the view of a soul, the view of a human, the view of a manava, the view of an agent, or the view of an experiencer.

It is impossible that anyone could receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate these, or extensively proclaim, reveal, and attend to them with correct mental application for the sake of others.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Any place where this sutra is expounded shall become a site for the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others to offer worship, pay homage, and circumambulate clockwise, just as they would a shrine of the Buddha."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family upholds, recites, masters, and thoroughly penetrates this sutra, and extensively explains, reveals, and attends to it correctly for others, yet should encounter slight contempt or even extreme contempt."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

These sentient beings have committed various impure karmas in their past lives that would otherwise result in rebirth in the evil destinies; however, because they encounter contempt and disparagement in their present life, all those impure karmas from their past lives are completely exhausted, and they shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Subhūti!

I recall that in the past, beyond countless kalpas and even further beyond the countless, prior even to the time of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, I encountered eighty-four koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand Buddhas, all of whom I served and attended; having so served them, I never committed any transgression against any of them.
"Subhūti! I have served all such Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and having served them, I have never committed any transgression against them.

If, in a future time, in a future period, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is about to perish, there are sentient beings who receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate this sutra, and who extensively proclaim, reveal, and correctly attend to it for the sake of others."

"Subhūti! My previous accumulation of merit cannot approach even a hundredth part of this accumulation of merit; likewise, it cannot approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-koṭi part, nor a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta part. It cannot approach any numerical fraction, any calculated fraction, any reckoned fraction, any illustrative fraction, nor even a *upaniṣad* (proportional) fraction."

Subhūti! If I were to fully describe the mass of merit produced by those sons or daughters of good family at that time, and even the mass of merit encompassed by those sons or daughters of good family, sentient beings would become bewildered, their minds confused and deranged.
Therefore, Subhūti, this Dharma gate taught by the Tathāgata is inconceivable and immeasurable; one should aspire to the inconceivable maturation it brings forth.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle abide?”
"How does one practice?
How does one subdue the mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle should give rise to this thought:

‘I shall cause all sentient beings to enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of wondrous nirvana without remainder; yet, although I have thus delivered all these sentient beings to extinction, there is not a single sentient being who has attained extinction.’”
Why is that? Subhūti!
If the notion of a "sentient being" arises in bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they should not be called bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Why is this? If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not be said to have the perception of a sentient being (sattva-saṃjñā) arise, it should be known that the same applies to the perception of a life-principle (jīva-saṃjñā), the perception of a person (pudgala-saṃjñā), the perception of a spirit (manuja-saṃjñā), the perception of a human (mānava-saṃjñā), the perception of an agent (kāraka-saṃjñā), and the perception of an experiencer (vedaka-saṃjñā). They should likewise not be said to have these perceptions arise.
Why is that? Subhūti!
There is not even the slightest dharma that can be called "one who has set out on the bodhisattva vehicle."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Did the Tathāgata, in the past, receive even the slightest dharma that could be realized as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara?"
When he had spoken these words, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there was not even the slightest dharma by which the Tathāgata, in the past, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.”
When he had spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"Subhūti! When the Tathāgata was formerly in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, there was not the slightest dharma by which he could realize anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi."
Why is that? Subhūti!

If there were even the slightest dharma by which the Tathāgata could have realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, then the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me the prediction, saying:
“‘O Māṇava, in a future age you shall be named Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Subhūti!

Because there is not the slightest dharma by which a Tathāgata can realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for this reason the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, bestowed upon me the prediction, saying:”
"O Māṇava, in a future age you shall be named Śākyamuni, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this so? Subhūti!
The term "Tathāgata" is a synonym for true suchness (*tathatā*);
the term "Tathāgata" is a synonym for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) which is non-arising;
the term "Tathāgata" is a synonym for the path of eternal cessation.
The term "Tathāgata" is a synonym for ultimate non-arising.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
If there is truly no arising, that is the supreme meaning. "Subhūti!
If one were to say that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha can realize anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, you should know that such a statement is not true."
Why is that? Subhūti!
It is because they slander me by giving rise to false attachments.
Why is this? Subhūti!
There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has been able to realize as anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi.

Subhūti! Regarding the dharmas realized by the Tathāgata in person, or the dharmas he has taught, or the dharmas he has contemplated—within these, they are neither true nor false. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
"Subhūti! As for 'all dharmas, all dharmas,' the Tathāgata has said they are not all dharmas; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them by the designation 'all dharmas, all dharmas.'"
The Buddha said to Subhūti,
“It is as if there were a man with a body, a great body.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding what the Tathāgata has called a person endowed with a body and a great body, the Tathāgata has said that it is not a body; for this reason, it is called being endowed with a body and a great body.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, So it is, Subhūti!”
If any bodhisattvas should speak thus:
"I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then they should not be called bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Is there even the slightest dharma that can be called a "bodhisattva"?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
“There is not even the slightest dharma that can be called a ‘bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“As for what is called a ‘sentient being,’ the Tathāgata has said that it is not a sentient being; therefore it is called a ‘sentient being. For this reason, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas have no sentient beings, no life-principles, no persons, and no individuals (pudgala), and so forth.”
"Subhūti! If any bodhisattvas should speak thus:
'I shall accomplish the meritorious adornments of a buddha-field.'"
It is also spoken thus. Why is this? O Subhūti!

Regarding the "adornment of the buddha-field by the merits of the buddha-field," the Tathāgata says it is not an adornment; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "adornment of the buddha-field by the merits of the buddha-field."

"Subhūti! If there are bodhisattvas who have deep faith and understanding in the dharma of selflessness as being the dharma of selflessness, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha declares them to be 'bodhisattva, bodhisattva.'"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do the Tathāgatas and others currently possess the fleshly eye?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata and others currently possess the fleshly eye.
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata currently possess the divine eye? Subhūti replied:
“So it is! World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatas and others truly possess the divine eye.”
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata and others currently possess the eye of wisdom? Subhūti replied, “It is so!”
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatas and others currently possess the wisdom-eye.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Do the Tathāgatas and others currently possess the Dharma-eye?”
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata and others currently possess the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!"
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata currently possess the Buddha-eye? Subhūti replied:
"So it is! World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatas and others truly possess the Buddha-eye."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
As for all the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, does the Tathāgata say that they are sand?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
The Tathāgata says that these are grains of sand."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, what do you think?”

Even as many as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, suppose there were that many rivers Gaṅgā; and even as many as there are grains of sand in all those rivers Gaṅgā, suppose there were that many world-systems.
"Would these worlds be considered many?
Subhūti replied, "Indeed they would!"
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"These worlds are exceedingly numerous.
The Buddha said, "Sudhana!"
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings in as many worlds as there may be, I am able to know the various individual streams of consciousness of each and every one of those beings.
Why is this? Subhūti!
As for the "streaming forth of the mind," the Tathāgata has said that it is not a streaming forth; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "streaming forth of the mind."
Why is that? Subhūti!
The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven kinds of precious jewels and offer them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, would the mass of merit produced by that son or daughter of good family on account of this cause and condition be great?"
Subhūti replied, “It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
“Very many, Sugata! The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
That son or daughter of good family will, by reason of this causal condition, generate a mass of merit that is exceedingly vast.
Why is this? Subhūti!
“If there were such a thing as a mass of merit, the Tathāgata would not call it a ‘mass of merit.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “What do you think?”
“Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the physical body as being perfect and real? Subhūti replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!
One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!
As for the ‘perfection of the form-body,’ the Tathāgata says it is not a perfection; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name ‘perfection of the form-body.’”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the possession of the various marks?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the various marks. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
"Endowed with all marks"—what the Tathāgata calls being 'endowed with all marks' is, in fact, not being endowed with marks; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as being 'endowed with all marks.'"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does the Tathāgata ever have such a thought:..."
"Do I have anything to teach? "Subhūti!
You should not view it in such a way."
Why is this? Subhūti!
If one says that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, that person slanders me; they have not correctly grasped my meaning.
Why is this? Subhūti!
As for "teaching the Dharma, teaching the Dharma," because no dharma can be apprehended, it is called "teaching the Dharma."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, in a future age, during the final period,

the last five hundred years, when the time for the extinction of the True Dharma is approaching, will there be any sentient beings who, having heard such teachings as these, are able to believe them with deep faith?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
They are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
All sentient beings are, according to the Tathāgata, not sentient beings; therefore they are called "all sentient beings."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Is there even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has fully realized as unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized as unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is so!”
"So it is! Within this, there is not even the slightest dharma that exists or can be attained; therefore, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
This dharma is equal; within it there is nothing that is not equal, and for this reason it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because it is equal in its lack of self-nature, lack of sentient-being-nature, lack of life-force-nature, lack of person-nature, and lack of pudgala-nature, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
There are no wholesome dharmas that are not directly realized, and there are no wholesome dharmas that are not perfectly awakened to. Subhūti!
As for "wholesome dharmas, wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata has declared them all to be non-dharmas; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them as "wholesome dharmas, wholesome dharmas."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to gather a heap of the seven precious treasures equal in measure to all the Sumeru Kings within a trichiliocosm, and offer it as a gift;

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, should even take up, uphold, read, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate a single four-line verse, and furthermore extensively proclaim, reveal, and attend to it with correct mental attention for the sake of others.

"Subhūti! The previously mentioned mass of merit cannot approach even a hundredth part of this mass of merit; likewise, it cannot approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-koṭi part, nor a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a reckonable part, nor a comparable part, nor even a fraction of a minute portion (upaniṣad)."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does the Tathāgata ever have such a thought as this:"
"Shall I deliver all sentient beings?
Subhūti, you should not view it in such a way.
Why is this? Subhūti!
There is not even the slightest sentient being who is delivered by the Tathāgata.

"Subhūti! If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, the Tathāgata would thereby possess the grasping of a self, the grasping of a sentient being, the grasping of a life-force, the grasping of a person, and the grasping of a pudgala, and so forth."
"Subhūti! What we call 'clinging to a self' the Tathāgata has taught to be non-clinging; therefore it is called 'clinging to a self,' yet foolish common worldlings stubbornly maintain this clinging."
"Subhūti! Those who are called 'foolish ordinary beings' by the Tathāgata are, in truth, not beings; therefore they are called 'foolish ordinary beings.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the possession of the various marks? Subhūti replied:
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the possession of various marks.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Excellent! Excellent! It is so!
"So it is! It is as you have said.
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of various marks."

"Subhūti! If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of his possession of the various marks, then a universal monarch (cakravartin) would also be a Tathāgata. Therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the possession of the various marks; rather, one should view the Tathāgata by means of the non-existence of the various marks."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who perceive me by my form, Or seek me through my voice, They have entered upon a wrong path; They are unable to see me as I truly am."
"One should contemplate the nature of the Buddha-dharma, which is the Dharma-body of the Teacher;
since the nature of phenomena is not an object of cognition, it cannot be fully understood.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the possession of the marks?
"Subhūti!..."
You should not now view it in such a way. Why is that? Subhūti!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the possession of marks.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
For one who has thus set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, is there any dharma established that is either destroyed or severed?
Subhūti! You should not view it in such a way.
"Those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle never posit even the slightest dharma as being destroyed or annihilated. Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River with the seven treasures and offer them to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the mass of merit arising from a bodhisattva who attains patient endurance regarding all dharmas that are selfless and unarisen would be far greater than that."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not grasp at a mass of merit.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why should a bodhisattva not grasp at a mass of merit?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! That which should be embraced and that which should not be embraced are therefore called ‘that which should be embraced.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
If anyone says that the Tathāgata goes, comes, stands, sits, or lies down, such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? Subhūti!
That which is called "Tathāgata" is a designation for reality and suchness; because he has nowhere to go and from nowhere does he come, he is therefore named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take as many worlds as there are atoms of dust in the great earth of a trichiliocosm, and were to turn the forms and images of those countless worlds into ink, like a mass of atoms."
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Would that mass of atoms be considered much?"
Subhūti replied, “That mass of atoms is vast indeed,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so, Sugata! Why is that?"
World-Honored One!
If an aggregation of atoms were substantially existent, the Buddha would not have spoken of it as an "aggregation of atoms. Why is this so?
The Tathāgata says that the accumulation of atoms is itself not an accumulation; therefore it is called the "accumulation of atoms.
The Tathāgata says that the trichiliocosm is itself not a world; therefore it is called the "trichiliocosm."
Why is this? World-Honored One!

If a world were a truly existent entity, it would constitute a grasping at a unified whole. The Tathāgata has said that grasping at a unified whole is itself no-grasping; therefore, it is called "grasping at a unified whole."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
This grasping at a unified whole is ineffable and beyond conceptual proliferation; yet all those foolish ordinary beings stubbornly cling to it as a real phenomenon.”
Why is this so? Subhūti!
If one were to say this:

“The Tathāgata has taught the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a person, the view of a soul, the view of a mind-born being, the view of a young brahmin, the view of an agent, and the view of an experiencer.”
"What do you think? Is what has been said thus correct speech? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
"Sugata! What has been said in this manner is not correct speech. Why is that? Because..."

The Tathāgata has taught that what are called the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a person, the view of a pudgala, the view of a mind-born being, the view of a manava, the view of an agent, and the view of an experiencer are in fact not views; therefore they are termed the "view of a self" up to the "view of an experiencer."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle should know all phenomena in this way, should see them in this way, and should resolve with faith in them in this way; thus they do not dwell upon the notion of phenomena."
Why is this? Subhūti!
That which is called "the perception of phenomena" has been taught by the Tathāgata as being non-perception; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "the perception of phenomena."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to fill immeasurable and incalculable worlds with the seven kinds of precious jewels and offer them as gifts to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, should even take up, uphold, recite, master thoroughly, attend to according to the principle, and extensively proclaim, reveal, and explain to others even a single four-line verse, the mass of merit arising from these causes and conditions would be far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
How does one proclaim and reveal it to others?
Because it is not proclaimed or revealed to others, it is therefore called "proclaiming and revealing to others."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All things produced through combination Are like stars, a cataract, a lamp, and a magical illusion;
Like dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud— One should contemplate them in this way."

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard the sutra spoken by the Bhagavān, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 577.
